title: World's First Air-Breathing Satellite Thruster Set for Orbital Test
summary:
The era of satellites that can "live off the land" in orbit is approaching. Kreios Space, a Spanish company, has announced plans to launch the first satellite equipped with an air-breathing electric propulsion (ABEP) system. This groundbreaking technology could revolutionize operations in very low Earth orbit (VLEO), the region between 60 and 250 miles above our planet.

In VLEO, residual atmospheric drag is a constant challenge. Traditional satellites carry limited fuel to counteract this drag, which restricts their operational lifespan. ABEP offers an elegant solution: the satellite scoops up ambient air molecules, heats and ionizes them into plasma, and then accelerates the plasma out to generate thrust. Essentially, it uses the atmosphere as propellant, enabling sustained flight without depleting onboard fuel.

"Kreios is building the satellites that make sustained operations in very low Earth orbit possible," said CEO Adrián Senar. "By enabling satellites to fly lower, longer and more efficiently, we are enabling higher-resolution Earth observation, much better satellite communications, and a more sustainable orbital infrastructure." The company has partnered with Kongsberg NanoAvionics to provide the satellite bus for the mission. While no firm launch date has been set, Kreios's website targets 2027. This test could pave the way for a new class of satellites that deliver unprecedented data quality and connectivity while reducing space debris, as VLEO satellites naturally deorbit more quickly at the end of their lives.
why_it_matters: Cheaper, longer-lasting satellites in VLEO could bring faster internet to remote areas and sharper climate data, while also helping to clean up space junk—issues that will directly affect the generation growing up today.

background_read: Most Earth observation satellites orbit much higher, around 400–800 km, to avoid air drag; VLEO (60–250 miles) has been avoided because even thin atmosphere would quickly pull a satellite down without constant thrust.
The idea of an air-breathing electric thruster was tested on the ground by agencies like the European Space Agency, but no spacecraft has ever flown with it.
Kreios Space, a Spanish startup founded in 2019, aims to be the first to demonstrate this technology in orbit.
They have partnered with Kongsberg NanoAvionics, a Lithuanian small satellite manufacturer, to supply the satellite bus—the core structure that houses power, communication, and control systems.

Using VLEO also helps tackle the growing space junk problem: satellites in such low orbits naturally re-enter the atmosphere within a few years even without power, unlike higher-altitude debris that can linger for decades.

perspectives.description: Earth observation companies and climate scientists would gain high-resolution imagery at lower cost, while telecommunications could see reduced latency for global internet. This could make vital data more widely available.

The technology is unproven in space; air-breathing thrusters may struggle with extremely low gas densities and contamination. A failure could discourage investment in VLEO and set back progress by years.

The push toward VLEO reflects a broader industry trend to optimize orbits for specific jobs while addressing sustainability. The same physics that causes drag also offers a natural way to dispose of satellites, turning a problem into a feature.

If ABEP succeeds, it could lead to permanent very-low-orbit constellations for real-time disaster monitoring, planetary missions that harvest local atmospheres, and even new regulations to prevent overcrowding in these valuable low bands.
